# Problem 1
```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(p8105.datasets)
data("ny_noaa")
```

```{r}
summary(ny_noaa)
```

This dataset has `r nrow(ny_noaa)` and rows and `r ncol(ny_noaa)` columns. Each row represents one measurement of New York weather from one weather station. Columns include `id`, identifying which weather station the measurement came from, `date`, the date of measurement in year-month-day form, `prcp` represents precipitation in tenths of mm, `snow` represents snowfall in mm, `snwd` represent snow depth in mm, `tmax` and `tmin` give the max and minimum temperature respectively, measured in tenths of degree C. Missing data is extensive, with `pcrp`,  `snow`, and `snowd` having somewhere between 100,000 and 600,000 NA values each, and `tmax` and `tmin` both having 1,134,358 NA values each.

```{r}
ny_noaa = ny_noaa |> 
  mutate(
    year = lubridate::year(date),
    month = lubridate::month(date),
    day = lubridate::day(date)
  )
```

Since snowfall and snow depth are in mm, while precipitation is in tenths of mm, I changed the precipitation to be in mm. Also since the both temperature variables are char variables in tenths of degrees C, I converted them into numeric variables in degrees C.

```{r}
ny_noaa = ny_noaa |> 
  mutate(
    prcp = prcp / 10,
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10
  )
```

```{r}
ny_noaa |>  count(snow, sort = TRUE)
```

Most common value for `snow` is 0 mm, which has 2,008,508 observations. This makes sense since snow in New York is generally limited to winter, so the majority of days throughout the year will not see snow. The second most common value is NA, with 381,221 values. This could be due to faulty equipment, or that some stations do not measure snowfall.



```{r}
ny_noaa |> 
  filter(month == 1 | month == 7) |> 
  group_by(year, month, id) |> 
  summarize(
    tmax_mean = mean(tmax, na.rm=TRUE)
  ) |> 
  filter(!is.na(tmax_mean)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y=tmax_mean, group=id)) + 
  geom_line(alpha = 0.25) +
  facet_grid(. ~ month) +
  labs(title = "Average Max Temperature for each Station over time",
       x = "Year",
       y= "Average High Temperature (degrees C)"
         )
  
```

We see that average temperature is lower in January than July, as expected. There is also no clear trend in temperature from 1980 to 2010 for either months. We see that from year to year, the average temperature fluctuates, but, with the exceptions of several outliers, all stations move in the same direction. The range of temperature across all stations is also consistent from year to year, with a rougly 10 degrees Celsius difference between the station with the highest and lowest average temperature. The most noticable outlier was around 1987, when one station saw recorded an average temperature in July of 14 degrees Celsius, with no other stations close to this value.

```{r}
tmax_tmin_hex = ny_noaa |> 
  filter(!is.na(tmax) & !is.na(tmin)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x=tmax, y=tmin)) +
  geom_hex() + 
  labs(
    title = "Max temperature vs Min temperature", 
    x = "Max Temperature (Degrees c)",
    y = "Min Temeprature (Degrees C)"
  )

library(ggridges)
snowfall_ridge = ny_noaa |> 
  filter(snow > 0 & snow < 100) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = snow, y=factor(year))) +
  geom_density_ridges() + 
  labs(
    title = "Snowfall Distribution by Year", 
    x = "Snowfall between 0 and 100 mm",
    y = "Year"
  )
  
library(patchwork)
tmax_tmin_hex + snowfall_ridge
  
```


## Problem 2


```{r}
covar = read_csv("data/nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4)
accel = read_csv("data/nhanes_accel.csv")
```
Cleaning Acceleration data
Converting sex 1 and 2 to male and female and education 123 to less than high school, high school equivalent, and more than high school
```{r}
covar = covar |> 
  mutate(
    sex = factor(
      sex,
      levels = c(1,2),
      labels = c("male", "female")
    ),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c(1,2,3),
      labels = c("less than high school", "high school equivalent", "more than high school"),
      ordered = TRUE
    ) 
  )

```

Get requirements and join with accel

```{r}
covar = covar |>
  filter(age >= 21) |> 
    drop_na()
nhanes = left_join(covar, accel, by = "SEQN")
```

Using inline r, tail(names(nhanes)) shows the last column names, since names() truncates
pivot longer for accel so instead of a bunch of min_x rows, you have a min column with entries x and mims with accel values

```{r}
nhanes_tidy = pivot_longer(
  nhanes,
  min1:min1440,
  names_to = "minute",
  names_prefix = "min",
  values_to = "MIMS"
) |> 
  mutate(minute = as.integer(minute))
```

Making first table

```{r}
nhanes |> 
  group_by(sex, education) |> 
  summarize(
    count = n()
  ) |> 
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex,
    values_from = count
  ) |> 
    knitr::kable()
  
```

```{r}
nhanes |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = age)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  facet_wrap(education ~sex) +   
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Age by Sex and Education",
    x = "Age",
    y = "Number of People"
  )
 
```
The age distributions are generally uniform across sex and education groups, although there are more participants with greater than a high school education. This group also seems to skew younger, with a larger proportion of participants at younger ages.

```{r}
nhanes_total = nhanes_tidy |> 
  group_by(SEQN, age, sex, education) |> 
  summarize(
    total_activity = sum(MIMS, na.rm = TRUE)
    )
```

```{r}
nhanes_total |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~education) +
  labs(
    title = "Total Daily Activity by Age",
    x = "Age",
    y = "Total Daily Activity",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```
In general, total daily activity decreases with age. Among participants with less than a high school education, this decline is the sharpest, although there is an uptick around ages 50–60 for men and a smaller corresponding increase for women. However, given the relatively small sample size, these fluctuations could be due to outliers. For those with a high school equivalent education, activity peaks around age 40 for both sexes, decreases until approximately age 60, and then levels off. Among participants with more than a high school education, activity remains relatively stable from ages 20–60 before declining at older ages. Women generally have higher total activity than men in the high school equivalent and more than high school groups.

```{r}
nhanes_time = nhanes_tidy |> 
  group_by(education, sex, minute) |> 
  summarize(
    mean_MIMS = mean(MIMS, na.rm = TRUE),
  )
```


```{r}
nhanes_time |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = minute, y = mean_MIMS, color = sex)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(. ~education) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(0, 360, 720, 1080, 1440),
    labels = c("12 AM", "6 AM", "12 PM", "6 PM", "12 AM")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Activity Throughout the Day",
    x = "Time of Day",
    y = "Average MIMS",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```
Across all three education levels, the general pattern is similar. Activity is lowest during the night, reaching its minimum around 4 AM, before increasing rapidly between 6 AM and noon. Activity generally peaks around noon, remains relatively high until 6 PM, and then steadily declines throughout the evening. The high school equivalent and more than high school groups show similar patterns, with activity remaining fairly constant between noon and 6 PM. In contrast, the less than high school group reaches a higher peak around noon, followed by a more gradual decline throughout the afternoon and a sharper decrease after 6 PM.
